description: Alkaline water electrolysis operating at 60-90°C with MW-scale commercial deployment and flexible operation capability.
summary: Currently dominant market technology alongside PEM with mature commercial deployment. Operates at 60-90°C with baseline electric efficiency of 55.1 kWh_el/kg_H2 (range 47.5–75.0). System CAPEX 790.5 €/kW with stack replacement at 48.9% of CAPEX. Stack lifetime approximately 75,532 hours.

description: Alkaline water electrolysis long-term future with improved efficiency and reduced capital costs.
summary: Long-term future development showing improved performance. Electric efficiency 48.9 kWh_el/kg_H2 (range 45.47–52.0). System CAPEX reduced to 527.2 €/kW, representing 33% reduction from near-term. Stack replacement 48.8% of CAPEX. Stack lifetime approximately 87,500 hours.

description: Proton exchange membrane electrolysis operating at 60-90°C with MW-scale commercial deployment.
summary: Currently dominant market technology alongside AEC with mature commercial deployment. Operates at 60-90°C with baseline electric efficiency of 57.9 kWh_el/kg_H2 (range 48.8–83.0). System CAPEX 1047.9 €/kW with stack replacement at 42.0% of CAPEX. Stack lifetime approximately 64,026 hours.

description: Proton exchange membrane electrolysis long-term future with improved efficiency and significantly reduced capital costs.
summary: Long-term future development with significant cost reduction. Electric efficiency 53.1 kWh_el/kg_H2 (range 47.0–64.0). System CAPEX reduced to 473.5 €/kW, representing 55% reduction from near-term. Stack replacement 39.4% of CAPEX. Stack lifetime approximately 85,420 hours.

description: Solid oxide electrolysis operating at 700-850°C with high-temperature thermal integration and natural gas heat input. Not yet commercialized at scale.
summary: High-temperature electrochemical process below thermoneutral conditions. Operating temperature 700-850°C. Baseline electric requirement 34.1 kWh_el/kg_H2 (range 26.6–38.1) plus thermal energy 8.3 kWh_th/kg_H2 (range 6.7–11.0). System CAPEX 1739.5 €/kW with stack replacement at 27.0% of CAPEX. Stack lifetime approximately 30,308 hours. High lifecycle GHG emissions from natural gas input for steam generation.

description: Solid oxide electrolysis long-term future with improved stack lifetime and reduced capital costs.
summary: Long-term future development with significantly improved economics. Electric efficiency assumed 34.1 kWh_el/kg_H2 and thermal energy 8.3 kWh_th/kg_H2 (same as near-term). System CAPEX reduced to 958.3 €/kW, representing 45% reduction. Stack replacement 13.8% of CAPEX. Stack lifetime improved to approximately 71,991 hours. Economic advantage of 42-218 €/t in Netherlands but negligible benefits in Chile (3-11 €/t reduction).

description: Low-temperature direct air capture using temperature-vacuum swing adsorption with amine-functionalized sorbent. Energy consumption varies significantly with ambient conditions.
summary: Temperature-vacuum swing adsorption process. Baseline electricity requirement 0.48 MWh_el/t_CO2 (range 0.25–0.70) and heat <100°C at 2.53 MWh_th/t_CO2 (range 1.75–3.30). Sorbent consumption 7.50 kg/t_CO2 (minimum 3.00) at cost 21.5 €/kg_sorbent (range 13.0–30.0). System CAPEX 730.0 €/t_CO2/year. Location-dependent performance factors from 1.00 (Iceland) to 1.69 (Spain) for CAPEX. Reference application: Climeworks Mammoth plant at 36 kt_CO2/year.

description: Low-temperature direct air capture long-term future with significantly improved sorbent efficiency and reduced energy requirements.
summary: Long-term development with improved performance. Baseline electricity requirement 0.38 MWh_el/t_CO2 (range 0.25–0.50) and heat 1.50 MWh_th/t_CO2. Sorbent consumption reduced to 3.00 kg/t_CO2 at significantly lower cost of 7.4 €/kg_sorbent (range 1.8–13.0). System CAPEX reduced to 237.0 €/t_CO2/year. Sorbent cost decline and consumption reduction attributed to 33.4% of total MSP reduction from near to long-term future.

description: High-temperature direct air capture using aqueous absorption process with energy-intensive calcination requiring natural gas.
summary: Aqueous absorption DAC process with natural gas-driven high-temperature calcination. Carbon footprint of CO2 feedstock estimated at 100 kg_CO2eq/t_CO2 (typical range 20–300 depending on absorption process). Minimum selling prices 21.5% higher than low-temperature DAC in near-term due to energy-intensive calcination. No cost advantage over point-source capture in this period. Lower data granularity compared to low-temperature DAC.

description: High-temperature direct air capture long-term future development with potential improvements but without clear cost advantages.
summary: Long-term future outlook shows high-temperature DAC does not offer distinct advantages over low-temperature adsorption DAC despite natural gas utilization. No cost benefits identified compared with LT-DAC in long-term horizon. Technology development constrained by fundamental energy requirements and calcination processes.

description: Postcombustion CO2 capture from industrial flue gas using amine-based absorbents. Typical capture cost of €50/t_CO2 for hard-to-abate industries like cement production.
summary: Point-source capture uses amine-based absorbents to extract CO2 from industrial flue gas with an average capture cost of €50/t_CO2. PSC products average 50% cheaper than LT DAC alternatives in the near term and may emit 10.9% more GHGs. The process serves as a catalyst for technological advancement while DAC capacities remain limited. Carbon footprint of captured CO2 is typically 100 kg_CO2eq/t_CO2.

description: Postcombustion CO2 capture for long-term future scenarios post-2035. Benefits from electricity cost reductions though cost differences versus DAC diminish.
summary: Long-term PSC performance is driven by electricity consumption dominance for downstream electrolysis. Cost advantages versus long-term DAC diminish as relative importance of capture cost decreases. CO2 emissions from fossil-based PSC do not lead to net-zero emissions even if considered climate neutral in regulations.

description: Fischer-Tropsch synthesis via reverse water-gas shift (RWGS) route converting CO2 to FT-fuel with intermediate CO production capacity of 229.3 kt/y and final output of 116.4 kt_FT-fuel/y.
summary: Two-stage Fischer-Tropsch synthesis via RWGS produces CO as intermediate product from 360 kt_CO2/y input. RWGS unit CAPEX is €28.4M baseline (range €14.4–42.5M), FT synthesis CAPEX is €100.1M baseline (range €44.9–195.8M). MSP ranges 1150–1750 €/t_product with cost per ton CO2 avoided of 543–1969 €/t_CO2eq,av. Life cycle GHG emissions are 55–88% lower than fossil diesel counterpart (44.3 MJ/kg LHV, 4164 kg_CO2eq/t).

description: Long-term Fischer-Tropsch via RWGS with MSP 2.5–3.3 times higher than fossil counterpart and improved cost reduction from electrolysis efficiency and sorbent improvements.
summary: Long-term FT synthesis via RWGS maintains MSP of 1150–1750 €/t_product (2.5–3.3 times fossil price). Cost per ton CO2 avoided improves to 225–537 €/t_CO2eq,av baseline range. Major cost reduction drivers include electricity cost reduction (~20% of MSP reduction), electrolyzer efficiency improvements, and sorbent cost/consumption decline (33.4% of total). Location performance shows Chile cheapest at 5% lower than Spain, 15% lower than Iceland, 45% lower than Netherlands. Most optimistic scenario achieves less than 1.5 times fossil price.

description: Direct methanol synthesis from CO2 and hydrogen with production capacity of 246.6 kt_methanol/y from 360 kt_CO2/y input and CAPEX of €120.2M baseline.
summary: Direct-route methanol synthesis from CO2 and hydrogen produces 246.6 kt_methanol/y from 360 kt_CO2/y input. CAPEX baseline €120.2M (range €59.0–181.9M). MSP ranges 580–840 €/t_product with cost per ton CO2 avoided of 543–1969 €/t_CO2eq,av. Life cycle GHG emissions are 65–91% lower than fossil counterpart (19.9 MJ/kg LHV, 1870 kg_CO2eq/t, fossil price 261 €/t).

description: Long-term methanol synthesis with improved economics reaching MSP 2.2–3.0 times fossil price and cost per ton CO2 avoided below 230 €/t_CO2eq,av.
summary: Long-term methanol synthesis maintains production of 246.6 kt_methanol/y with MSP 580–840 €/t_product (2.2–3.0 times fossil price). Cost per ton CO2 avoided improves to 225–537 €/t_CO2eq,av baseline range, estimated to fall below 230 €/t_CO2eq,av. Life cycle GHG emissions remain 65–91% lower than fossil counterpart. Economics align well with existing EU climate change mitigation policies and incentives. European Refining Association estimates long-term cost at 400–650 €/t_CO2eq,av.

description: Methanation synthesis from CO2 and hydrogen producing 124.6 kt_methane/y from 360 kt_CO2/y input with CAPEX of €36.8M baseline.
summary: Methanation synthesizes methane from CO2 and hydrogen, producing 124.6 kt_methane/y from 360 kt_CO2/y input. CAPEX baseline €36.8M (range €27.8–41.7M). MSP ranges 1050–1730 €/t_product with cost per ton CO2 avoided of 543–1969 €/t_CO2eq,av. Life cycle GHG emissions are 62–94% lower than fossil counterpart (49.8 MJ/kg LHV, 3984 kg_CO2eq/t, fossil price 166 €/t). For SOEC operation, 90% methane boiler efficiency would require ~41.6 kt_CH4 reused to reduce life cycle GHG emissions (~1/3 of produced methane).

description: Long-term methanation with MSP 6.3–8.9 times higher than fossil counterpart, representing the highest multiplier among major CO2 conversion products.
summary: Long-term methanation maintains MSP 1050–1730 €/t_product (6.3–8.9 times fossil price). Cost per ton CO2 avoided improves to 225–537 €/t_CO2eq,av baseline range. Life cycle GHG emissions remain 62–94% lower than fossil counterpart. Methanation faces the highest cost challenge relative to fossil counterpart among major products examined due to its high energy requirements.

description: Dimethyl ether synthesis from CO2 and hydrogen producing 186.7 kt_DME/y from 360 kt_CO2/y input with CAPEX of €85.7M baseline.
summary: Dimethyl ether synthesis from CO2 and hydrogen produces 186.7 kt_DME/y from 360 kt_CO2/y input. CAPEX baseline €85.7M (range €53.6–135.7M). MSP ranges 695–1060 €/t_product with cost per ton CO2 avoided of 543–1969 €/t_CO2eq,av. Life cycle GHG emissions are 77–96% lower than fossil counterpart (28.8 MJ/kg LHV, 2304 kg_CO2eq/t, fossil price 356 €/t). Geographic performance shows Chile has lowest production costs.

description: Long-term dimethyl ether synthesis with MSP 2.2–3.0 times higher than fossil counterpart and improved cost competitiveness through policy incentives.
summary: Long-term DME synthesis maintains MSP 695–1060 €/t_product (2.2–3.0 times fossil price). Cost per ton CO2 avoided improves to 225–537 €/t_CO2eq,av baseline range, estimated to fall below 230 €/t_CO2eq,av. Life cycle GHG emissions remain 77–96% lower than fossil counterpart. Economics align with existing EU climate change mitigation policies. Geographic performance shows Chile ~5% lower than Spain, 15% lower than Iceland, 45% lower than Netherlands.

description: Ammonia synthesis via Haber-Bosch process using hydrogen from renewable electrolysis and CO2 from low-temperature solid sorbent direct air capture.
tech_type: Haber-Bosch with DAC-sourced CO2 and renewable H2
summary: Haber-Bosch process converting CO2 and renewable hydrogen to ammonia. Plant operates 8000 h/year with 277.4 kt ammonia/year capacity based on 360 kt CO2/year input. Baseline capital cost €132.2M (range €107.9–€165.8M). Hydrogen production specific energy: AEC 55.1 kWh/kg, PEM 57.9 kWh/kg, SOEC 34.1 kWh/kg electric + 8.3 kWh/kg thermal. Investment lifetime 25 years with 1.5 debt-to-equity ratio. Life-cycle GHG emissions 72–96% lower than fossil-based ammonia (~107–740 kg CO2 eq/t depending on location and electrolyzer). Minimum selling price ~410–670 €/t long-term. Cost of CO2 avoided: 203–1087 €/t CO2 eq near-term.

description: Long-term projection (2050) of ammonia synthesis via Haber-Bosch with renewable hydrogen and CO2 capture, showing improved technology maturity and reduced costs.
tech_type: Haber-Bosch with DAC-sourced CO2 and renewable H2
summary: Haber-Bosch ammonia synthesis in long-term future with full commercialization. Same 8000 h/year operation producing 277.4 kt/year. Electrolyzer capital costs significantly reduced: AEC €527.2/kW (range €306.5–€774.5), PEM €473.5/kW (range €257.9–€700.5), SOEC €958.3/kW (range €566.5–€1723.3). Improved hydrogen efficiency: AEC 48.9 kWh/kg (45.47–52.0), PEM 53.1 kWh/kg (47.0–64.0). Electrolyzer stack lifetimes: AEC 87,500 h, PEM 85,420 h, SOEC 71,991 h. Minimum selling price 410–670 €/t (54.2% reduction from 2035). Life-cycle GHG emissions 72–96% reduction vs fossil (74–740 kg CO2 eq/t). Cost of CO2 avoided: 110–266 €/t CO2 eq. Geothermal (Iceland): €25.6/MWh with 13.9 kg CO2 eq/MWh.

description: Standard Haber-Bosch process for ammonia synthesis from hydrogen and nitrogen extracted from air via air separation unit.
summary: Standard Haber-Bosch ammonia synthesis with hydrogen from water electrolysis and nitrogen from air separation. Plant operates 8000 h/year (ramp-up: 30% year 1, 70% year 2) producing 277.4 kt ammonia/year. Baseline capital cost €132.2M (range €107.9–€165.8M). Investment lifetime 25 years with 1.5 debt-to-equity ratio. Location-dependent cost factors from Iceland baseline: Netherlands +29%, Spain +45%, Chile +17%. Long-term minimum selling price 410–670 €/t. Life-cycle GHG emissions 72–96% lower than fossil-based ammonia. Netherlands shows lowest emissions (~6% lower than Iceland, 50% lower than Spain, 55% lower than Chile). Cost of CO2 avoided near-term: 203–1087 €/t, long-term: 110–266 €/t.

description: Urea synthesis via conversion of ammonia and CO2, where ammonia derives from Haber-Bosch and CO2 from low-temperature direct air capture.
summary: Urea synthesis converting ammonia and CO2 to urea product. Plant operates 8000 h/year (ramp-up: 30% year 1, 70% year 2) with 491.8 kt/year capacity (highest among assessed products). Baseline capital cost €50.1M (range €24.6–€74.2M). Investment lifetime 25 years. Location-dependent cost variations from Iceland baseline: Netherlands +29%, Spain +45%, Chile +17%. Long-term minimum selling price 360–510 €/t with Chile lowest cost, most cost-competitive with fossil counterparts (<2.5x for most locations). Life-cycle GHG emissions 68–89% lower than fossil-based urea. Fossil benchmark: €202/t, 1406 kg CO2 eq/t (2020). Cost of CO2 avoided: near-term 203–1087 €/t, long-term 110–266 €/t (below 230 €/t aligns with EU climate policies). Discount rate 5–8%, scaling factor 0.6–0.9.

description: Thermally integrated process converting methanol to mixed olefins through optimized heat integration, compressors, and separation units.
summary: Methanol-to-olefins (MTO) conversion with thermal integration optimization. Plant operates 8000 h/year (ramp-up: 30% year 1, 70% year 2) producing 93.8 kt/year mixed olefins. Baseline capital cost €92.1M (range €77.0–€107.1M), includes compressors, heat exchangers, and separation units. Investment lifetime 25 years. Location-dependent advantages in long-term: Iceland baseline, Netherlands/Spain/Chile competitive. Long-term minimum selling price 1515–2240 €/t (among highest-cost products); Chile ~5% lower than Spain, 15% lower than Iceland, 45% lower than Netherlands. Life-cycle GHG emissions (cradle-to-grave) 50–87% lower than fossil olefins (benchmarked against EU PET plastic: 60% recycling, 20% incineration, 20% landfilling). Netherlands (offshore wind) shows lowest emissions due to electricity consumption significance. Cost of CO2 avoided: high variability near-term (€5062–26739/t CO2 eq), long-term 395–1730 €/t. SOEC sensitivity: Netherlands 42–218 €/t MSP reduction, Chile 3–11 €/t. Discount rate 5–8%, scaling factor 0.6–0.9.
